title: Why does a tiny GPS time error put you so far off? | So That's Why
description:
Little Q was walking to the park to meet her classmates. Between two rows of tall buildings, the blue dot on her phone map suddenly jumped to the street across the way, and when she reopened the map, it took ages to come back. How does a phone use time to know where you are?

In this episode, the Chief and Little Q follow one walk and think it through with a "whistles in the park" game: how late you hear a whistle tells you how far away that friend is. Satellites are friends carrying atomic clocks, and their signals travel as fast as light, so a time error of just a millionth of a second means 300 meters of distance error, and even the tiny relativity difference in the satellites' clocks has to be fixed first. A phone has no atomic clock, so it listens to a fourth satellite and works out how far off its own watch is, too. Next they look at why the dot drifts: the satellites send very precise signals, and what flings the dot across the street between buildings is mostly buildings blocking signals and walls bouncing them. The ionosphere high up also slows signals, but it changes slowly across the whole sky and doesn't suddenly jump between buildings; part of it can be corrected, and listening to two frequencies at once removes almost all of it. Finally: why you wait when you first open the map, how phones use the network to skip the wait, and why some phones then need one more satellite.

Drawing circles to find where they cross is only a diagram; a real receiver works out position and time together. The illustrations were made with AI; they are diagrams, not real satellite positions. The source of every claim is listed in the references below.

Information as of 2026-11-11
